name: Onakantheeswarar Temple, Kanchipuram
deity: Shiva as Ona Kantheeswarar, worshipped with the goddess Kamakshi in the Kanchipuram tradition
period: Ancient Shiva shrine of Kanchipuram sung in the Tevaram (8th century); structural temple with later additions
summary: Ona Kantheeswarar, the Tiru Onakanthan Thali of the Tevaram, is one of the ancient Shiva shrines of Kanchipuram, known for the three lingas within its walls and for the two devotees, Onan and Kaanthan, whose names it carries.

sections.history: Within the sacred city of Kanchipuram stands the shrine of Ona Kantheeswarar, sung by the saints and so a Paadal Petra Sthalam; in the hymns it is called Tiru Onakanthan Thali. The temple takes its name from two figures of its legend, Onan and Kaanthan, remembered in tradition as commanders of the army of the asura king Banasura, who are said to have worshipped the Lord here and given the shrine its enduring name. The temple stands in the Panjupettai quarter of the city, its shrines raised on an elevated platform, and it is kept in worship under the state endowments board, one of the smaller Tevaram shrines of a city dense with ancient sanctuaries.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered beneath a small three-tiered rajagopuram, and its shrines stand together on a raised structure. Its distinctive feature is the presence of three Shiva lingas, each in its own sanctum — two held in tradition to be the lingas worshipped by Onan and Kaanthan, with a third associated with the temple's legend. The presiding linga is honoured as swayambhu, self-manifested, and behind it the Lord and the goddess are shown together in the posture of their sacred marriage, the tirumana kolam. In keeping with the Kanchipuram tradition, the Mother Goddess is worshipped as Kamakshi.
sections.legends: The legend of the shrine turns on its two namesakes, Onan and Kaanthan, commanders in the service of the asura king Banasura. Drawn to devotion, they are said to have obtained a linga and worshipped Shiva at this spot, and from their names the Lord came to be called Ona Kantheeswarar and the shrine Tiru Onakanthan Thali. The three lingas of the temple are read in tradition as the signs of this devotion, and the shrine keeps the memory of those who turned from their former nature to the worship of the Lord. Accounts of the legend differ in their details from source to source.
sections.festivals: The temple observes the festivals of the Shaiva year — Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham, and the days sacred to Shiva — in the manner of Kanchipuram's older shrines. As the dates follow the Tamil calendar, it is best to confirm them locally before a visit.
sections.experience: Ona Kantheeswarar is one of the smaller, quieter Tevaram shrines of Kanchipuram, and a visit here has the feeling of coming upon an old sanctuary tucked within the living city. Come before the three lingas within their sanctums, pause at the sacred-marriage image behind the Lord, and let the shrine take its place in a wider round of the city's Paadal Petra temples.

visit.timings: Typically open for limited hours in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the Panjupettai area of Kanchipuram. The town is well served by rail and road, about 75 km from Chennai, whose international airport is the nearest; local buses and autos reach the quarter. Ask locally for the Onakanthan Thali shrine, as Kanchipuram holds many temples of similar name.
